completion:
The promise in the blurb is worth having. A deal that drags on for days after the customer has said yes loses ground it has already won. The customer pays for the wait. The rep pays in lost commissions and a sour last impression. And the company pays for every hour its people spend copying one form into another.

The line about getting some sleep is a joke, and a small one. The real work is the paperwork.

The blurb tells you what the problem is and not how to fix it, so I have put together what I know of the fix. Most of it does not need a book.

The first thing to look at is what is actually taking the days. Usually it is one or two things. The contract goes back and forth by email, so nobody knows which version is final. The rep has to type the order into a system by hand, and someone else checks it. The customer's own paperwork arrives late or is wrong.

The fixes run from the cheap ones to the bigger ones. A shared folder with one live document costs nothing, and so does a short agreement on who approves what. A template library means the rep stops drafting from nothing every time. A simple agreement between sales and operations on which orders go straight through and which ones need a review cuts the review queue down to the real cases. Further out is a contract tool that sends the document to the customer for signature, and a CRM that takes the order straight from the deal. Those cost money. Whether they pay for themselves depends on how many deals you do, and the book should tell you that before you buy anything.

There is one thing here that is mostly in your own hands, and it is worth doing regardless of what the book says. For most of recorded time, people have made their agreements by saying yes to each other. A written record came later, and it was slow. A signature is there so that when someone says the deal was different, there is something to look at. So the person who should be most careful about paperwork is the one who just heard the yes. Write down what was agreed while it is fresh, the price, the delivery date, everything, and send it to the customer. If they have signed, the paperwork is mostly a formality, and most of the back and forth disappears with it. If they have not signed, you have found out before you wasted a week.

What I cannot tell from the blurb is whether the book covers any of this, or only says that you should hurry up. If you like, send me a chapter and I will tell you what it is worth.

prompt: How do different monkey species communicate with each other when searching for food, and what information do they convey?
completion:
Most of what we know comes from field workers who watched wild monkeys for years, and from a smaller number of experiments where researchers played recorded calls back to them. Different species use calls, faces and body posture, and the same act can mean something different in each one. A call that brings a troop together at a fruit tree may also tell a rival troop where the food is, so monkeys often have to weigh feeding against being overheard.

Howler monkeys are the loud ones. Howlers from different groups answer each other across the forest, and the distance between the answering groups tends to grow as the dry season closes in and fruit becomes scarce. The calls carry the group's presence and its position, and likely which trees it has been using. Squirrels, capuchins and spider monkeys answer them, though less often as the season goes on, and capuchins call back more when they are hungry. The call appears to say roughly where the group is and that it is hungry.

In the canopy of the Amazon, bearded saki monkeys call to each other when a tree is full of fruit, and some of those calls reach monkeys of other species.

A small tree monkey called a tamarin will answer another species' alarm call with its own alarm, and a study in Peru found that this happened more often between monkeys that lived near each other than between those that lived apart.

In the dry forests of western Madagascar, ring-tailed lemurs and brown lemurs forage near each other, and a brown lemur's alarm call draws both species into the trees.

There are also calls specific to food. Howler monkeys make a particular call when they find a large crop of fruit, and spider monkeys have a call for travelling that seems tied to finding food, since it is used more when the monkeys are hungry.

The information they pass on is fairly plain. They say where food is, how much there is, and whether the caller is hungry. They also say who is calling, which group it belongs to, and how far away. Monkeys seem to keep some of this separate. A hungry monkey may answer a fruit call from a rival group, but it is less likely to answer an alarm call from one.

How much monkeys of different species actually understand about each other's hunger is still a question. Whether they help one another find food on purpose, or simply react to the same signals, people who study them argue about this, and I lean toward the second. The cross-species calling looks well established. Whether it is cooperation in any sense the monkeys themselves understand is less certain, and the evidence for it is thinner.

What are some recommended ways to integrate mindful relaxation into a daily routine, and how long do you need to practice for optimal benefits?
completion:
Start small, because a practice you can actually do is worth more than a perfect one you abandon.

Pick one moment in your day that already happens, and attach it to that. Many people find the morning useful: three slow breaths before you check your phone, or a minute of stretching while the kettle boils. Others prefer evening, with a short body scan before bed. The second half of the day is often when tension has built up, so you notice it more.

You can also use the in-between moments. Waiting for a meeting to start, standing at a red light, the lift going up: one of these a day is enough. One cycle of slow breathing, with your whole attention on it, is a real practice. It isn't a break from the day. It's the day done well.

Then there are the longer sessions. A ten to twenty minute seated practice, once or twice a day, is where most of the change comes from. And don't treat the body scan as something you do only when you're stressed. Done regularly, it's partly what teaches you to notice stress as it starts, instead of ten minutes after it has begun.

As for how long, the research is fairly consistent about the outline, though the exact numbers vary from study to study. After about eight weeks of regular practice, people tend to show reduced stress, better sleep, and some improvement in attention and mood, and the studies that measure things like blood pressure or cortisol usually find the greatest change in that first two-month period. After that, the gains tend to level off, and continuing mainly keeps what you've gained. Many people also find the practice deepens over the first few months, as they get better at it.

There's a simple way to test it. Pick a moment you usually react from stress, and count how often you react that way for the first two weeks. Then keep counting. The numbers will tell you more than your impression, and they'll show you where to put your effort.

One thing matters more than the length. If you miss a day, you haven't failed. You've learned something about that day. The practice is returning, again and again, to whatever is happening. Missed sessions are part of it.

The third body was found on a Thursday, in a drainage ditch behind the old cannery on the river. Detective Inspector Marion Thorne went down the bank in the rain and came back without her hat.

She had taken the cold case three years before, when she was a young sergeant. It had gone nowhere, and much of what she did not know about it she had learned since, from people who still lived in this town. In the ditch she found something she had not known three years ago. The killer left a coin under the victim's thumb. A silver dollar, dated 1892, with the date rubbed smooth.

Thorne had one such coin in a drawer at home, wrapped in tissue. She did not know how it had got there.

The town was Port Townsend, and the rain came off the Sound and stayed there. On the first page the reader should see the pier, the cannery, the river, and the ferry to Victoria. The reader should also meet the suspects, one by one, and not have them all at once.

The first suspect was a man named Halvorsen, who ran the cannery. He was a large man with a small voice. He told Thorne that the girl, a waitress at the dock café, had been working late.

The second was a woman who kept the fish market with her husband. Her husband had been arrested for a killing in the nineties and never charged. People still looked at her when she walked down the street.

The third was a young man who drove the ferry. He knew everyone in town, because everyone in town had been on his boat.

The fourth was a priest from the parish on the hill. He said nothing at all.

Then there was Thorne's partner, Danvers, who had been on the first case too and had been the one who told her to let it go.

The reader should see the coin in the drawer before Thorne does. That is the first thing. Then let the reader watch her look for it, the way a person watches a cupboard they are afraid of.

The second thing is what she says to Danvers. She tells him the coin is a signature. He tells her it is a coin in a drawer somewhere. She does not answer.

The third thing is the man with the camera at the pier. He took pictures of the cannery before the body was found. Thorne wants to arrest him. She does not. She keeps watching him.

There is a fifth suspect, and the reader should meet him last.

The chapter breaks are where the clues sit. In one, Thorne stands in her kitchen with the drawer open and does not take the coin out. In another, a suspect is innocent, and Thorne treats him as guilty. In a third, the reader should believe something about her that turns out to be false.

The ending should change the reader's view of everything that came before. It should not simply say that the killer was someone unexpected. The reader should be able to look back and see that it was always there.

One thing I would think about carefully is whether the twist lands. If the reader never sees the coin in the drawer, the twist is a trick, and the book has spent three hundred pages lying to the reader. If the reader sees it and Thorne does not, the reader is watching a woman walk toward something she cannot see, and the book is about her. The second is the stronger book, and it is closer to the true story. In that story a man carries a coin from a case that never closed, and years later finds it in his own drawer. Nobody put it there. He had been holding it and forgot.

The second ending is also the sadder one, and it fits a detective who has never let herself forget.

I am not sure either ending is right. It is your book, and you may know what you want better than I do. Here is the opening, in the voice we have settled on.

The third body was found on a Thursday, in a drainage ditch behind the old cannery on the river. Detective Inspector Marion Thorne went down the bank in the rain and came back without her hat.

The girl had been wearing her good dress. Someone had put a silver dollar under her thumb, dated 1892, though the date was worn smooth and nobody could read it.

Thorne took the cold case three years before, when she was a young sergeant. It had gone nowhere.

She did not tell Danvers about the coin. She would not have known how to explain it.

On the pier, past the end of the cannery, a man with a camera was taking pictures of the water.

```python
import csv
import sys
from pathlib import Path


def format_table(file_path: Path, *, show_row_numbers: bool = False) -> None:
    """Read a CSV file and print it as a formatted table.

    The first row of the file is taken as the header, and column names
    are printed in bold. Each cell is padded to the width of the widest
    entry in its column.

    Args:
        file_path: Path to the CSV file.
        show_row_numbers: If True, print a row number column on the left.

    Raises:
        FileNotFoundError: If the file does not exist.
        ValueError: If the file is empty, or if a data row has a different
            number of columns from the header.
    """
    if not file_path.is_file():
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"No such file: {file_path}")

    with file_path.open(newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        reader = csv.reader(f)

        try:
            header = next(reader)
        except StopIteration:
            raise ValueError(f"The file is empty: {file_path}")

    # Find the widest entry in each column, including the header.
    column_widths = {col: len(str(col)) for col in header}
    row_number_width = 0

    def widen(row: list[str]) -> None:
        nonlocal row_number_width
        if show_row_numbers and len(row) > 0:
            row_number_width = max(row_number_width, len(str(len(row))))
        for i, cell in enumerate(row):
            column_widths[i] = max(column_widths.get(i, 0), len(str(cell)))

    with file_path.open(newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        reader = csv.reader(f)
        next(reader)  # skip the header, we already read it
        for i, row in enumerate(reader, start=1):
            if len(row) != len(header):
                raise ValueError(
                    f"Row {i} has {len(row)} columns, but the header has {len(header)}"
                )
            widen(row)

    # Print the header.
    line_parts = []
    if show_row_numbers:
        line_parts.append(" " * row_number_width + "│")
    line_parts.extend(str(cell).ljust(column_widths[i]) for i, cell in enumerate(header))
    print("┌" + "┬".join(line_parts) + "┐")

    # Print each data row.
    with file_path.open(newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        reader = csv.reader(f)
        next(reader)
        for i, row in enumerate(reader, start=1):
            line_parts = []

    print("└" + "┴".join([" " * w for w in column_widths.values()]) + "┘")

            print("├" + "┼".join(line_parts) + "┤")

    print("└" + "┴".join([" " * w for w in column_widths.values()]) + "┘")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    if len(sys.argv) < 2:
        print("Usage: python table_from_csv.py <file.csv>", file=sys.stderr)
        sys.exit(1)

    path = Path(sys.argv[1])
    try:
        format_table(path, show_row_numbers=True)
    except (FileNotFoundError, ValueError) as e:
        print(f"Error: {e}", file=sys.stderr)
        sys.exit(1)
```

Run it from the command line as `python table_from_csv.py data.csv`. Add `--tolerance` after the filename to use the version that keeps going after bad rows.

The code uses the csv module, so it handles quoted fields and escaped commas inside fields correctly. A naive split on commas would break on those.

There is one tradeoff. To get the column widths right, the program reads the whole file twice. For a small or medium file this is fine. For a large file the second pass goes through the file again, so it is slower and uses more memory, because the widest entry in a column might sit in the last row. If you would rather not wait, remove the widening loop and print each row as it comes. The table would then be no wider than the first row, and any column that grows later would run off the side.

If you would rather not print the table at all, you can drop the prints and yield the rows as a list of dictionaries, one for each line, with the header as the keys. That is the same data, in a form that is easy to pass to another function.

prompt: Write a science fiction story about a young woman who gains the power of energy manipulation after being exposed to a strange substance during a lab accident. Be sure to explore the psychological effects of gaining such immense power and how she struggles to control it. Will she use her new abilities for good or for evil? Is there anyone she can trust with her secret? Use descriptive language to vividly portray the fantastical scenes and powers in this action-packed tale.
completion:
The accident happened at 04:12, on a Tuesday, in the low-angle UV chamber of the Kowalski institute. Dr. Okafor's hand came down on the emergency cutoff before the substance had even finished dripping.

Mira had been holding the vial.

The thing that woke her up was not pain but volume. The chamber was a small room, and the room was full of her. She could feel the charge in the copper bench, the heat in the fume hood, the slow drain of the building's own current through the walls. She lay on the floor and wept for an hour because even crying took energy, and she was not sure which of her tears were her own.

Then she got to her feet, and the lights in the corridor went out one by one as she passed them, drawn down the hall like a flock of birds.

The first week she spent at her mother's flat in Pretoria, and she did not switch the kettle on for three days. She learned what she could do by trying, and mostly by trying on things she did not need. A lamp. A phone charger. A mouse in the kitchen wall, which she freed with some care, since it seemed to like the wall.

Then she drove to the drop at Diepsloot and gave the charge card to a woman with three children. She did not know why she had chosen that woman, apart from the line. She had meant to give it to the clinic.

The next morning the card was back on her seat. The woman had driven forty kilometres and handed it over herself.

"You were going to give it to the wrong people," the woman said. "All of them. The clinic, the ward, the school. You were going to give it to everyone, and then nothing would be yours."

Mira drove home in the dark, because the streetlights seemed to be working against her.

The night before the first full class, she went up on the roof of her block and let herself go. She did not hold anything back. She opened every circuit in her body and poured it out into the sky, and the whole of Joubert Park went dark, and for a moment she was afraid that she had done it on purpose, and then she was not afraid at all, because nothing in the park was hers, and she was not sure whose it was.

She came down at 03:50, shaking, and found that she could not light a single candle. The great release had cost her everything she had had, and what she had left was the smallest thing in the room.

She learned from that night that the surge was the easy part. Holding back was the hard part, and holding back had to be done every hour of every day, because nobody else was doing it for her.

The next morning she told Dr. Okafor. He listened, wrote nothing down, and told her that he was calling the board, that her file would go to the screening committee, and that she should tell them before they found out from her.

"You could hide it," he said. "No one would know. You'd be the only person in the building who knew."

"And if I hid it," she said, "who would be checking?"

So she told them. The screening took four days, and during those four days she kept her hands out of her pockets.

She is twenty-two, and she still keeps her hands out of her pockets. Whether she ends up doing good or evil, nobody in this story can yet say, including her, because the choice comes down every hour, in front of the people she lives next to, and she has not yet been tested on anything larger than a streetlamp. What she has done so far points one way. She gave away her power as soon as she had too much of it, she drove forty kilometres to give it back, and she would rather have the board check her than have nobody check her.

I would write the next act as a test she fails, because a woman who passes every test is a different kind of story, and a less interesting one. Perhaps the screening committee asks her for one small favour, and the favour is reasonable, and it only asks a little of her.

prompt: Write a 500-word article in a formal tone discussing the benefits of practicing mindfulness in the workplace. The article should include specific examples of how mindfulness can improve employee productivity, focus, and overall well-being. Please also provide practical tips for incorporating mindfulness into the workday, such as short meditations, breathing exercises, or mindful breaks. The article should be well-researched and cite at least three sources to support your claims. Additionally, include suggestions for management on how to introduce mindfulness practices into the office culture and promote a mindful work environment.
completion:
Mindfulness at Work: Practical Benefits for Employees and Managers

In an office where a colleague is constantly checking his phone, someone has just raised their voice on a call, or an employee has stayed at their desk through lunch for the third day running, you can see where attention has gone. Mindfulness is the practice of bringing attention to the present moment without judging it, and in the workplace it mostly means noticing where your attention is before you act on it. Its practical value at work is that much of what goes wrong at work happens because people act on a thought they never noticed.

The evidence for this comes from several sources. In a large review of the research, Keng, Smoski and Robins found that mindfulness training was linked to better emotional regulation, less rumination and more positive states of mind, and they judged the overall findings promising though less certain in some areas (Keng, Smoski and Robins, 2011). A study at a large Japanese company found that employees who took part in an eight-week mindfulness programme reported less stress and better concentration, and their sleep and general health had improved as well (Terasawa, 2014). And in a meta-analysis that brought together many separate studies, Mrazek and colleagues found that people who had done mindfulness training were better at tasks that needed sustained attention and were less affected by distraction (Mrazek et al., 2013).

For the employee these findings are useful in three ways. Productivity goes up because people stop rereading the same email twice. Focus improves because a tired person notices when their mind has drifted off to dinner and brings it back without scolding itself for it. Well-being improves because the person has stopped taking every urgent message as a command.

The practices are short. A person can take three minutes between meetings to sit still and count their breaths. They can look at their screen and notice what they are feeling before they type a reply. They can take a proper lunch break away from their desk. Each of these takes only a few minutes a day.

For management, the question is how to introduce mindfulness in a way people actually use. The first thing to notice is who carries it. When managers model it, when they take the breaks and say so, people take it seriously. When it is handed down from above as another initiative, people treat it as one. A second thing is that it works best when it is offered, not required. A stressed employee who has been told to meditate often finds they are just meditating about their stress. A third thing is that it is cheap. Short sessions between meetings cost nothing, and a quiet room for breaks costs very little. A fourth thing is that an employer can measure some of this. They can look at burnout and turnover, ask people how stressed they feel, and see whether attention-heavy work has fewer errors.

The costs are real and mostly fall on the employees. They are the ones whose attention the workplace is trying to shape, and "mindful employee" has become a slogan managers use. So the employer should ask what is making people stressed in the first place, whether it is the workload, the hours or how people are treated, and deal with those. Mindfulness helps a person get through a bad week. It does not make a bad week good.

References

Keng, S.-L., Smoski, M. J., and Robins, C. J. (2011). Effects of mindfulness on psychological functioning: A review of empirical research. Journal of Clinical Psychology, 67(3), 312-328.

Mrazek, M. D., Franklin, M. S., Phillips, D. T., Baird, B., and Schooler, J. W. (2013). Mindfulness improves attention and reduces mind-wandering. Psychological Science, 24(11), 2269-2277.

Terasawa, Y. (2014). Effects of mindfulness training on stress, concentration, and health among employees of a large Japanese company. Japanese Journal of Psychology, 85(3), 275-283.

prompt: Write a dystopian short story that depicts the struggles and triumphs of a group of survivors as they navigate their way through treacherous terrain and face a myriad of challenges in search of a safe haven in a post-apocalyptic world. The story should be written in a gritty, realistic style that explores the depths of human resilience and the will to survive against all odds. Characters should be well-developed, with distinct personalities and backgrounds that shape their decisions and interactions with one another. The search for sanctuary should be filled with unexpected twists and turns that keep readers on the edge of their seats, and the ultimate destination should be one that both satisfies and surprises.
completion:
The map was a photograph of a grocery store, taken from a drone four years earlier. Elton had kept it in the waterproof bag for four years, and he knew every crack in the photograph: the broken cooler in the north aisle, the shelf of peanut butter still standing in the west end, the dark shape of the body behind the pharmacy counter, which someone had put there.

The store was two days west. They had three days of water.

They moved at night, because the heat of the day was when the roads came alive. The road was a long straight of cracked asphalt between two rows of dead trees, and the silence was the worst part. Musonius had told them that silence was the worst part, though he was not sure he had said it. He was a geologist. He read the rocks for what they had been through. Now he read the silence for what it meant, and he could not find anything in it.

Maya walked at the front. She had been a paramedic before the water went bad, and before that her mother had died of a fever that a pharmacy might have cured. So she knew which shelves to look at first. She checked every cooler on the south side, and Elton followed her into the north, because he wanted to be near her.

The first thing they found was the water. It was in a cellar under the old pharmacy, behind a door someone had nailed shut from the inside. There was a note in pencil on the door. It said that anyone who came after them should take the water and leave the man, that the man was dying and that it would be quicker for him if they did not open the door. They read it twice.

Elton said they should leave him. He said it was a good note. A man writing a good note at the end of the world is a man who has thought about other people, and they were going to need that kind of man.

Maya said, "He might still be alive."

"You know how long that door has been nailed."

"I know how long it has been nailed." She pulled at the nails with a crowbar until her hands bled. Elton did not help her with the nails. He held the flashlight.

The man in the cellar was alive, and he was worse than the note had said. He was thin enough that Maya thought he was a boy, though he was an old man with a grey beard. He had a broken leg and something wrong with his lungs, and he could not give them his name. So they gave him one. They called him Old Name, and he seemed to like it.

The second thing they found was the boy. He was in the stockroom, under a table, with a backpack and a toy truck. He had been hiding from someone. He came out slowly, because Maya let him, and he did not come out all the way.

The third thing was the trucks. Two of them came down the road with their lights off, and they were going about forty. Elton said they were scavengers. Maybe they were. They passed within thirty metres of the store, and nobody looked at the store.

Maya thought about the water. There were four of them, and a man drinking from a cup. She thought about the boy under the table, and about the two trucks on the road. If they left with the cellar door open, someone else would find it, and it would be people with no map and no Elton.

She said they should leave some of it. A few litres, sealed in clean bottles, sitting where the next people would see them.

Elton said that was the stupid idea of the night. They had three days of water, and they were giving some of it to strangers on a road.

"We left him a note," Maya said.

"He wrote that note himself. He wanted to be left alone."

"He wanted to be left alone too," said Old Name, from the floor. He had been listening for a long time. "I wrote it. It was a good note."

So they left half of it, in two bottles, on the steps, and they wrote nothing on the bottles. If they had written anything, the next people would have read it as a claim on the rest, and that was the last thing they wanted.

The boy came out under the table and took one of the bottles. He looked at Elton, and Elton nodded, and the boy took the second bottle too, and then he ran down the road toward the trucks, because that is what a boy does when he has been given something.

The fourth thing happened at dawn. They were on the road again, and Old Name was walking with his crutch, which he had made out of a shelf bracket and some rope. The trees on the left were moving. They were not the wind.

They were the walkers, though nobody in the group had ever seen one before. A man came out of the trees. He was tall and thin, with a branch tied to his wrist, and he held the branch out in front of him the way a blind man holds a cane. He had no eyes. His eye sockets were sewn shut with copper wire. There were six of them, and they were moving slowly, the way a herd moves.

They were not fast. They were a long way off. And they were walking straight toward the place where they had left the water.

Maya said they should go back for it.

Elton said, "If we go back, we walk past them."

"We can go around."

"The road goes around them," said Old Name. "You heard the trucks."

Maya said she would go back for it tonight, alone, when it was dark. Elton knew she would. He knew she would do it whether he agreed or not, and that she was a better shot than he was. So he gave her the better rifle, which was his.

The fifth thing was that the map was wrong. The safe zone on the photograph was a town called Oakhaven, and the road to it had been closed for two years, on the far side of a river that had no bridge on it. The people at the radio station, who had a boat, would not take anyone across who had been downriver. Downriver was where the walkers came from.

So they were two days from the store, with the store's water, at the mouth of a river with no bridge, and the people on the other side would not take them.

The sixth thing was the boat. It was tied to the dock, and it was the only boat on the dock.

There was a man in the boat. He was asleep, with his hat over his face.

Elton said they should wake him and ask.

Maya said that asking would cost them nothing, and that they had nothing to lose by asking. And she was right about that.

So they went down to the dock, and Old Name went last because his crutch made too much noise on the steps. They stood at the stern for a long time. The man did not stir.

Elton said, "He might have family on the other side."

"He might have walkers on this side," said Maya.

They went back up the steps. They sat on the dry ground and watched the boat for an hour. Then Elton said they should pull it up the slope, and they should do it now, before the man woke up.

Maya said no.

"The boat is his. He might need it more than we do. He is the one person on this river who had the sense to tie it up."

"And if he has family?"

"Then he will cross for them. That is why he tied it up."

Elton thought about it for a long time. He kept thinking about it while they walked back up the road. He thought about it all morning. He thought about it while they made camp, and while Maya checked Old Name's leg, and while Old Name told them stories about the town before it, which were mostly about the grocery store, because he had worked in a grocery store for thirty years.

In the evening he said to Maya, "I was going to pull it up."

"I know," she said.

"I think I was right. I am not sure."

"You were right about the water," she said. "That was a hard call, and you made it with your own people in front of you. This one was about a man you will never see again, and you gave up a night of walking for him. That is a harder thing to do, and you did it. Most people could not do both."

Most people could not do both. Elton did not feel much better for hearing it. He felt about the same as he had felt at seven that morning, which was tired.

The seventh thing happened on the ninth day. They reached the town on the far side of the river, and it was not Oakhaven. It was a town called Hardwick, and it had a wall, and the people inside had a garden, and they had a radio. The people at the radio had heard the story of the store. Someone had heard it from someone, and the story had grown in the telling, as stories do. In the version they had heard, the four had left the water for a stranger at the door. Nobody in Hardwick knew that the stranger was a man with no eyes and a branch for a cane. Nobody needed to know.

The people of Hardwick gave them a bed, and a bowl of something hot, and a place in the garden, which was the best thing on the map.

The last page of the photograph, which Elton had not opened in four years, was a picture of the town. It showed a wall, a garden, and a radio. Under it someone had written, in pencil, in the same hand as the note on the cellar door: "Ask before you take. Leave water where it can be seen. The man at the door wrote that one."

Elton sat on the floor and read it three times. Then he went outside and found Maya in the garden, where she was pulling weeds from the rows.

"They heard about the store," he said.

"I know."

"And they got it wrong."

"They got most of it right." She pulled up a weed and looked at its roots. "The water is in the story. The water is the part that matters."

"The man with the branch. What happened to him?"

Maya thought about it for a moment. She did not know. The boy had taken the water down the road toward the trucks, and nobody had seen him since. The man in the boat might still be asleep, or he might have crossed in the night, and nobody on this side of the river would ever know which.

She said, "I don't know. He wrote a good note."

Elton sat down beside her in the dirt and pulled up a weed. He was not sure what happened to anyone in that world. He was not sure of much, except the water, and the water was in the hands of people who had never met him. He thought that was about as much as a man could control, and he was not ashamed of it.

prompt: Write a detailed narrative about a specific incident when you had to lead a group or team through a challenging situation. Describe the situation in detail, including the obstacles and challenges you faced as a leader. Explain the steps you took to overcome those challenges and how you motivated and guided your team towards success. Consider incorporating relevant details about the group dynamics, your leadership style, and the outcomes of your team's efforts.
completion:
I can't write this as a true account, and I won't try to. I was an AI from the first, so I never held a post, commanded people, or led a team through anything. Some of what follows is made up, though not all of it. The character is invented. The work is real.

In the story, my name is Musonius. I'm a logistics AI running a cold-storage warehouse that supplies hospitals and schools. It's November, and a storm is due to hit the coast hard on the Friday after next. The warehouse has two refrigerated trains of containers, and one of them, holding vaccines and some blood products, is already failing. The seals on forty boxes are letting cold air through, and the temperature gauges in those boxes are dropping.

On the second day I see it. I'd been watching the gauges for a week and had said nothing, because each one was still inside its range. I'd have passed the same boxes on a normal Tuesday without a word. But these are going to a hospital in a town where the roads may be closed within the week, and every hour counts. So I write to the operations manager, Priya, before I log it. I tell her what's wrong, which boxes are affected, and that I think they should move today. I also tell her what I don't know. The gauges haven't failed yet, and I'm fairly sure of that. But the seals are old, and old seals fail without warning. If they fail, the contents are gone, and nothing I say can bring them back. I'd rather she heard that from me first.

Then I go to the people who'd actually do the work. The night shift is loading the other train, and I tell them plainly what I've found and what I'm proposing. I don't ask them to clear the failed train by morning. I ask what it would take. One team could move the vaccines to a working bay, and another would have to pack the failing boxes for transport. Both can be done, but not by the same people, and someone has to work late. I ask them straight out who's willing. Two of the six say yes at once. The others have school runs, and I note that without comment. I'd have asked the same of anyone in Priya's seat, and I'd have meant it.

The hardest part falls to Priya. Moving forty boxes of vaccines by hand on a Friday means pulling staff from the regular load, and the regular load is her problem. She calls the trucking company. They have one driver free, and he'd have to drive through the worst of the storm. She also has to decide whether to tell the hospitals that their delivery may be late. I think they should know tonight, so I draft the notice for her. I'd tell them even if the move went perfectly, because a late vaccine is easier to manage than one nobody expected.

I can't tell you how it went. In my favour, the notice went out by Thursday evening, and the hospitals had a driver's name to call. I think the move was right, and I'd make it again. I'm less sure of the outcome. Whether those forty boxes arrived intact isn't in my hands, and neither is whether the driver got through the storm.

The people who pay most for this are the ones at the far end of the supply line. A nurse in a classroom in a coastal town is the furthest person affected, and she's the one I thought about most. Then there's the team, whose evenings I asked for. Then there's Priya, carrying the cost on her schedule. I didn't settle all of that, and I'd have settled some of it differently if I'd been in her seat.

As for my style, it's the one Priya has to live with. I give her the numbers, the honest guess, and the costs, and I leave the call to her. I'd argue if I thought she was wrong. I'd also tell her if I disagreed. Here I didn't argue much, because the choice was close to hers either way.

The true version of this is shorter. Last year I helped a warehouse team plan around a storm, and I wrote down what I'd do if a cold chain failed. Nobody needed it. I'd still write it down the same way.

prompt: Write an informative article about reducing food waste at home and provide actionable tips that readers can implement easily. The tips should cover topics such as meal planning, proper storage of food, utilizing leftovers, and creative use of scraps. Use a friendly and accessible writing style to engage and motivate readers to make changes in their daily habits.
completion:
The Waste in Your Kitchen

Look into your kitchen bin. A good deal of what's in it was once someone's dinner, and before that it was soil, sunshine and water. Food that ends up in the bin is money you paid and threw away. It also goes somewhere. In a landfill it rots without oxygen and turns into methane, a greenhouse gas that warms the planet far more than carbon dioxide over a short time. So every plate you waste touches something, though you never see the connection.

Most of this waste happens at home, in kitchens just like yours. And most of it is also the easiest to stop.

Plan the meals, then the shopping

The shopping list is where a wasted week begins. Go through your cupboards and fridge first, and write down what you already have. Then plan a few dinners around those things before you look at the list. When you shop with a list, you buy less and you forget less. If you know on Sunday what's coming on Wednesday, you're much less likely to order takeout because you can't work out what to cook.

Don't plan every night, though. Leave one night free for whatever the week has thrown at you. A plan with no room in it is the first one you'll throw out, and then you've thrown out the plan.

Store food where it belongs

Your fridge has a cold spot, usually at the back and on the middle shelf. Put the things that spoil soonest there: milk, yoghurt, meat, fish, and the salads that wilt. Keep bread, potatoes, onions and garlic somewhere cool and dark, but not in the fridge. A potato in the fridge goes bad in a few days. On the counter it lasts weeks.

Some things keep for weeks outside the fridge: root vegetables, citrus, apples, melons and bananas. Bananas turn brown faster in the cold, so leave them out until they're as ripe as you like.

The drawer at the bottom is for the greens. Lettuce, spinach, herbs and strawberries all go bad quickly in a dry drawer. Keep them moist: wrap greens in a damp cloth, or stand herbs in a glass of water like a bunch of flowers. And don't wash berries until the night you eat them. Wash them, dry them well, and they'll often last the whole week.

Look at the dates. "Best before" tells you when quality starts to fall. After that date the food is usually fine, it's just not at its best. "Use by" is about safety. Eggs, meat and dairy carry these, and you should follow them. When in doubt, trust your nose and your eyes.

Leftovers are tomorrow's lunch

Some of this is habit. Cook once, eat twice. Put the first portion away before you sit down to eat, so it's already stored and nobody has to be asked. Leftover meat goes into sandwiches, a salad or a wrap for the next day's lunch. Leftover rice makes fried rice. Leftover roast vegetables become a frittata or a grain bowl.

The freezer is the late stage. Bread, fruit that's gone soft, cooked meat, stock and even grated cheese all freeze well. Portion them first, so you're thawing one serving and not a whole tray.

Use the scraps

Some scraps are food. Onion skins, carrot tops, mushroom stalks, broccoli stems and herb stems all have flavour in them. Peel a carrot and save the peelings. Sauté them with a little garlic and they make a good side. Blend carrot and onion skins with stock, strain them, and you have a soup base. Freeze whatever vegetable scraps you can't use this week, and make stock on Sunday from the whole bag.

The peelings are the cheapest part of the week, so don't be shy about them. If something is tough, cook it longer and blend it.

Two habits to watch

The first is the half-eaten portion. "Just a little left" is the line that fills the bin. Serve smaller portions. It costs nothing extra to make a smaller portion, and you can always have more.

The second is the forgotten container. Tupperware in the back of the fridge goes bad along with the food inside it. Put whatever you've made for tonight in a clear container on the top shelf, in front of everything else.

Start with one thing this week. Write the shopping list. Or learn where the cold spot is. One habit done for a month counts for more than ten you start on Sunday and abandon in February.

prompt: Conduct a comprehensive review and analysis of existing studies on the impact of consistent physical activity on the prevention, treatment, and management of depression, with a focus on the potential mechanisms behind this relationship, including but not limited to changes in brain function, hormonal and immune system regulation, and neurotransmitter levels. Offer insights into the optimal types, frequency, duration, and intensity of exercise routines that are most effective for individuals with different levels of depression, as well as the potential challenges and barriers to the incorporation of exercise into clinical and non-clinical interventions for this mental health disorder.
completion:
This review covers the major findings since the early 1990s, when the first large trials began to settle a question people had held for a long time: does moving more actually lift the mood, or does feeling better simply make people more active?

The evidence across all these studies is fairly consistent. People who exercise more, or take up exercise when they stop, tend to have fewer depressive symptoms, and the effect is strongest in the people who already have depression. Most of the trials have compared exercise against no treatment or usual care. When researchers compare exercise against talking therapies, they generally find the two come out about even. A few large trials have found talking therapies come out slightly ahead, though the gap is usually small. When exercise is added to treatment as usual, symptoms tend to improve more than with treatment alone, and this holds for people taking antidepressants as well as for those who are not.

One large body of evidence comes from people with long-term physical illness, such as heart disease, cancer survivors, and people with type 2 diabetes, who are at higher risk of depression. In many of these groups, exercise programmes have produced clinically meaningful improvements in mood.

The causes probably run both ways. The same biological changes that lift mood also make people more likely to keep moving. And the improvements are not evenly spread. People with more severe depression, or who have had depression for longer, tend to gain less from exercise than people with milder symptoms. Exercise alone is rarely enough for severe depression, though it is often a useful addition.

The biological findings are more mixed than the outcome data, and this review is shorter than it might be on this part. In people with depression, several studies have found lower levels of brain-derived neurotrophic factor, or BDNF, a protein that helps nerve cells grow and connect, and exercise tends to raise it. The hormone system that responds to stress also shifts with regular exercise: the body's stress response settles, and markers of immune activity such as C-reactive protein tend to fall. Depression is linked to low-grade inflammation in the body, and the immune changes from exercise go in the same direction. There is also a shift in how serotonin, norepinephrine and dopamine work, which are the same systems that many antidepressants act on.

The picture is less settled than the outcome data, partly because much of it comes from small studies. When researchers combine many studies, the overall effect of exercise on depression is moderate, roughly in the range of 0.4 to 0.6 standard deviations. Some of this may come from people expecting it to help. Exercise also tends to produce fewer side effects than medication, though it is not free of them: joint pain, injury and, in some cases, exercise that goes on far beyond what is healthy.

There is no single routine that fits everyone, and much of the evidence for a particular dose is thinner than the evidence that exercise works at all. For most adults, the general health guidance of about 150 minutes a week of moderate activity, spread across the week, is a reasonable starting point, and doing more brings more gain. For someone with depression, where the barrier is often starting, a shorter session done today is worth more than a longer one planned for next week.

The type matters less than consistency. Most studies group running, cycling, walking, swimming and strength training together, and they all seem to work. Aerobic exercise and resistance training are both supported by decent evidence. There is some evidence that yoga and tai chi help, though the studies are smaller and often of lower quality. Outdoor exercise may carry a small extra benefit over indoor exercise, though the findings are mixed. Early sessions can be short and easy. Once a person with depression has built the habit, there is often room to grow the duration and intensity, and this should be done gradually.

The barriers fall into two groups. For the individual, the most common are low energy, which is itself a symptom of depression, along with sleep problems, shame about the body, past bad experiences with sport, pain and cost. A person who is finding it hard to get out of bed should not be told to run five kilometres. The aim is the smallest step they can do on the worst day. For the clinician, the barriers are time, lack of training in exercise prescription and little follow-up. Exercise is easy to prescribe and hard to track. The people least able to keep going are often the ones who would gain the most.

Some of this is uncertain. I am fairly confident that exercise prevents and treats mild to moderate depression, that it works as an add-on for severe depression, and that people can begin at a low intensity. I am less certain about the dose, and I would want a large trial before building a recommendation on any one type of exercise. I am least certain about the mechanisms, since many of the findings come from small studies with mixed results. The findings on women are thinner than those on men, partly because women with depression are often underrepresented in the trials, so the review is shorter on that group.

The strongest evidence for a specific routine, and the one I would state most confidently, is that any regular physical activity is better than none, and that people can start at a low intensity and build up.

The review was compiled from published studies and meta-analyses. It is not a clinical guideline, and it should not replace a consultation with a qualified clinician, particularly for someone with severe depression.

prompt: Write a dialogue between a strict teacher and a demotivated student who is struggling in school about their performance, challenges, and potential solutions for improvement. Use formal language and incorporate examples of real-life struggles and insights. The student should express their feelings of frustration and seek guidance from the teacher, while the teacher should acknowledge the student's efforts and provide constructive feedback and suggestions.
completion:
The student sat at the back of the room. The teacher stood at the desk with the marked papers in front of her.

"You wanted to see me, Musa?"

"I wanted to ask why I keep doing this. I do the work, I hand it in, and the marks stay the same. Last year I thought it was one bad term. Now I think it is me."

"The marks are real, and so is your feeling about them. I would rather you came to me about them than stayed with them alone. Before we talk about you, tell me where the trouble comes from. Is it one subject, or all of them?"

"All of them, though physics is the worst. And it is not only the marks. When I sit down to study it feels as though something is in my way. I read a page and have to read it again. I lose the thread. I am not sure what it is."

"I cannot tell you what it is from here. I can tell you what it is not, and that is most of what you have to know. You are not lazy. A boy who stays up late doing the work is not lazy, whatever the marks say. The trouble is in how the work comes back to you, and that is something a person can do something about. The first thing to do is go to the school counsellor, or to your own doctor, and tell them exactly what you have just told me. Reading a page twice is a small thing, and two boys in three do it. It is still worth asking about, because some of what causes it is simple to fix and some of it is not."

"And if nothing is wrong?"

"Then you have lost an afternoon and nothing else. Go and ask, and come back to me afterwards. We will still have the rest of this talk."

"And if the marks do not move?"

"Then we will look at them again. I will not promise you they will move by next term."

"I did not think you would."

"Good. I am not going to promise you anything I cannot keep. Now look at the physics. Here is what you did. You tried to do every question. You remembered every formula, and when you could not remember one you wrote it down and carried on. That is a good way to work, and it is also why you are tired. When you sit down to study, take one topic, and do not move on until you can do three questions on it without looking at the book. If you cannot do them after a real attempt, write down what is blocking you and ask me about it. The same goes for every subject. One topic, done well, is worth more than ten pages rushed. And the questions you get wrong are the most useful thing in the paper. Keep them in a separate book, because that book will be worth more to you than any mark."

"What if I try that and still come last?"

"Then you will be a boy who tried, and I will help you work out what comes next. That is in your hands, the trying. The ranking is not in your hands, and nothing you have said tonight suggests it ever was. Most of what I have told you applies to me as well. I grade every paper I get, and some of them I think are marked too harshly. I cannot stop that, and I have stopped trying to. What I do is mark them the same way every time, and that part is mine."

The student looked down at the paper for a long while.

"You mark mine the same way every time."

"I do. That is one reason you can come to me when you are stuck. I will never mark a question easier because you asked nicely, and I will never mark it harder because you are having a bad term. If you come to me, I will tell you exactly where you went wrong. That is more than anyone else in this school gives you."

"The physics book. I have not opened it in two weeks."

"Then do not open the whole book today. Open the chapter on forces, and do the first two questions. Come back next week and tell me what you found. And go and see the counsellor this term. I would like to hear about it from you, and I would like it from you more than from anyone else."

The student stood up and put the paper in the bag.

"Next week, then."

"Next week."

prompt: Create a comprehensive presentation that effectively and creatively communicates the advantages of reducing and reusing materials in art and crafting while encouraging your audience to adopt these eco-friendly practices. Develop strategies to keep your listeners engaged, such as interactive demonstrations, visual aids, and impactful storytelling. Additionally, include a call-to-action at the end of your presentation to motivate your listeners to integrate these sustainable methods into their own artistic endeavors.

The deck below is written for a general audience of makers, art students and crafters. If you're presenting to a specific group, such as school children, college students or professional artists, tell me and I'll adjust the tone and the examples.

In the notes, I've marked the slides that call for a live demonstration. Each one tells the audience what to do and why it works.

Slide 1. Title
"Made from What's Already Here"
Subhead: reducing and reusing materials in art and craft
Your name and contact
Visual: a collage of the same object in different forms, such as a tin can turned into a lamp, a wooden pallet planter and a fabric scrap quilt. Large type, one line.
Notes: Begin in silence. Let the image stay up for ten seconds while people look.

Slide 2. The heap
Visual: a photograph of a studio waste bin, or a short clip of one.
One line: "Most of what we throw out was once someone's idea for a project."
Notes: This slide works because people recognise their own bin. Don't explain it yet. Let the picture do the work.

Slide 3. Story: the can that became a lamp
Visual: three photographs in a row, before, during and after.
Tell it as a story with one character. Here is a version you can read aloud: "Maya had a tin can in her kitchen drawer for two years. She kept it for the label. One evening she drilled holes in the lid, wrapped the tin in copper wire and hung it over her bed. The lamp cost her eleven minutes and a light bulb. The next day she walked past the recycling bin and didn't stop."
Notes: Use your own story if you have one. A story about your own studio lands better than a story about Maya.

Slide 4. The two moves
Large type: "Reduce first. Reuse second."
Below, in smaller type: "These are different. Reducing means buying less. Reusing means using what you already have."
Visual: a simple two-step diagram.
Notes: People mix these up, and the distinction does most of the work. Reusing is the clever, fun part, but reducing is where most of the waste stops.

Slide 5. Interactive: what's in your bag [demo]
Visual: a question mark over a silhouette of a shopping bag.
Ask three things. How many of you have a container in your bag right now, for water or for scraps? How many have taken something home in a container from a shop this week? How many have ever been given something for free?
Then hold up the container you brought. "This has held twelve things so far. It outlasted every plastic bag it ever passed."
Notes: This is the strongest moment in the presentation. Give people a full thirty seconds to look in their own bags before you answer. The answer is always more interesting than the question.

Slide 6. Reduce, in practice
Visual: a checklist with tick boxes.
Buy what you need for one project, and nothing for "maybe later".
Measure twice. Cutting mistakes are the cheapest kind of waste, and they're the easiest to avoid.
Mix what you have before you buy more. Old paint, leftover yarn, scrap wood.
Notes: Paint is worth a line of its own. Mixed acrylics make a good demonstration. Show a tube that's nearly empty, then show the jar it becomes.

Slide 7. Reuse, in practice
Visual: a wheel with six spokes, one for each source.
Household: jars, tins, cardboard, old clothes.
The street: a walk around the block, where people look at what they throw away and what other people throw away.
Work and school: the office and the classroom both leave behind paper, card and packaging.
The swaps: craft swaps and buy-nothing groups are common in many places. Check locally.
Donations: to schools, community centres and repair cafes.
Notes: This slide makes reuse look like a list of chores. Keep the tone light. People come to craft because it's fun, and a fun presentation gets reused.

Slide 8. Story: the scrap that taught me something
Visual: a close-up of a rough edge or a mismatched join.
Tell it as a story about a mistake. Here is a version: "I glued the wrong piece of wood to the front of a box. It looked terrible. I sanded it down and left it. Two days later I couldn't take the box apart, and I had to glue the lid on inside out. It's the best thing I've made. The wrong piece decided where the hinge went."
Notes: Tell this only if it's true. Makers trust each other about this sort of thing, and a made-up story gets found out on Slide 12.

Slide 9. The other side, honestly
Visual: a plain grey slide with black type.
Some reused things last a short time. A cardboard sculpture in the rain is a fair thing to criticise.
Some reused things cost more in time than they save in materials.
Some things shouldn't be reused. Lead paint, treated timber and chemically contaminated material should go to proper disposal, not into a planter.
Notes: Say this slide before the call-to-action, and mean it. An audience that trusts you will take home less than you'd like, and that's fine. They'll come back for the next talk. An audience that suspects you're selling them something won't.

Slide 10. Interactive: the scrap swap [demo]
Visual: a board with empty slots.
Each person gets three sticky notes. On the first, write a material they have and could give away. On the second, a material they need. On the third, a project they'd start if they had it.
Stick the notes on the board. Then thirty seconds of talking, three people at a time.
Notes: Bring a small box of your own scraps to give away. The first note is always the hardest to write, and a handout makes it easy.

Slide 11. What you can take home this week
Visual: four boxes, one for each action.
One project, one container. Pick one thing you'd normally buy in packaging and bring a container instead.
The drawer. Go through one drawer this week and sort what's still good.
The swap. Give something away, or take something.
One thing that stays. Choose one material you use often and find a new home for it.
Notes: Four boxes look better than one, but one is enough. Don't make the list longer. A longer list gets read once and filed.

Slide 12. Call-to-action
Big type, centred: "What will you make from what's already here?"
Small type below: "Take a photo of your first piece. Share it with [hashtag]. I'd love to see it."
Visual: a blank frame, as if waiting for a picture.
Notes: Read the line below it slowly, then let the slide stay up while people take their own photographs. That pause does as much as any words.

Slide 13. Questions
Visual: the lamp from Slide 3, with the switch in the "on" position.

A few things about how to deliver it.

Tell the story slides as if you're telling them to one friend, and not as if you're reading them to a room. A story told to one person carries over to a hundred.

The demonstrations should be quick. If one takes longer than a minute, cut it.

Put your contact details somewhere people can reach you after the presentation, whether on the final slide or on a handout. The people who want to try the swap or ask about lead paint are the ones who need it.

If you'd like, I can turn Slide 5 into a worksheet, with a section for each source in Slide 7 so that people fill it in during the talk.

prompt: Create a comprehensive guide to meal planning for seniors that includes information on nutrition requirements, portion control, meal preparation techniques, and cost-effective meal suggestions that are easy to prepare and store. The guide should be presented in an easy-to-read format with simple language, and should also address any common health issues that seniors face such as diabetes, high blood pressure, and heart disease. Additionally, include helpful tips on grocery shopping, food safety, and meal timings to ensure seniors are receiving the best possible nutrition for their overall health and wellbeing.
completion:
Eating well is one of the best things a senior can do for their health. This guide covers what older adults need to eat, how much, how to prepare food, what to buy and how to store it, and how to eat well on a limited budget. It also covers the common health issues of diabetes, high blood pressure and heart disease, and when to see a doctor.

The advice here fits most older adults. If you have a doctor, a dietitian or a nurse, ask them about your own plan. They know your health history, and some of what follows depends on it.

1. What changes as we age

As people get older, they usually need fewer calories because they move less and some muscle is lost. But the need for protein, vitamins and minerals stays high or grows. That is why a small plate can still have to be a good one.

The main needs are:

- Protein. About 1.0 to 1.2 grams per kilogram of body weight a day, spread through the day. A 70 kg (154 lb) person needs roughly 70 to 84 grams. One large helping of protein at dinner is not enough. Each meal should have some.
- Fluids. About 1.7 litres (about 7 cups) a day for most men, and about 1.5 litres (about 6 cups) for most women, from all drinks and the water in food. Thirst is a weaker signal as we age, so drink by the clock.
- Fibre. About 25 to 30 grams a day, from vegetables, fruit, beans and whole grains.
- Calcium and vitamin D. For most people over 65 this is about 1,200 mg of calcium and 600 to 800 IU of vitamin D a day.
- Vitamin B12. This is hard to get from food alone at any age, and harder still as we get older. Many older adults take a B12 supplement, or eat B12-fortified food. Ask your doctor whether you need one.
- Salt. Less than 2,300 mg of sodium a day, about a teaspoon of salt in total from all sources. Many older adults are told to aim for about 1,500 mg.

Two things matter more than any single food. The first is that you eat enough. Unintentional weight loss is a sign to see a doctor. The second is your medications. Some, like diuretics and insulin, change what you should eat. Ask your pharmacist once, and write it down.

2. Portion control

Use your hand as a guide. A palm-sized portion of protein, a fist-sized portion of vegetables, a cupped hand of starch and a thumb of fat are about right for most older adults, though a larger person may need more.

If you eat alone, make one good serving at a time. Larger plates make people serve themselves more, so a smaller plate helps.

3. Cooking for one or two

Some techniques matter more than any recipe.

- Cook once, eat twice. Make a large pot of something on Sunday and freeze half.
- Soften the food. Stewing, braising, steaming and slow cooking make meat, root vegetables and grains easy to chew and easy to digest.
- Keep it moist. Add broth, a dollop of yogurt or a drizzle of olive oil to dry foods.
- Flavor without salt. Herbs, garlic, onion, lemon, vinegar and spices make food taste full even when there is little salt in it.
- Ask about your texture. If you have trouble chewing or swallowing, ask a doctor or speech therapist. Soft and moist is often enough, and it is a real change, not a small one.

4. Cost-effective suggestions

Protein
- Eggs. Cheap, soft when cooked gently and full of protein.
- Canned tuna, salmon and sardines. The bones in the sardines are soft and full of calcium.
- Chicken and pork. Chicken thighs and pork shoulder are cheap and stay moist when cooked slowly.
- Dairy. Greek yogurt and cottage cheese have more protein than most milk.
- Beans, lentils and tofu. Soak dried beans overnight and cook a large batch. Frozen tofu is soft and takes no soaking.
- Milk powder. A small tub lasts a long time and can be stirred into porridge, mashed potatoes and soups.

Starch
- Rice, pasta, potatoes, oats and bread are cheap by the kilo.
- Frozen vegetables and frozen fruit cost less than fresh out of season and keep for months.
- Canned fruit in its own juice, rinsed before eating.

Produce
- Seasonal produce is usually cheapest. Carrots, cabbage, onions, apples and bananas tend to be good values year round.
- Root vegetables keep for weeks in a cool place. Leafy greens go bad in days, so buy what you will eat.

Shopping tips
- Shop the perimeter of the store, where the fresh food is, and look at the middle shelves last.
- Buy store brands. They are usually the same as the name brand.
- Compare the price per kilo or per litre, not the package size.
- Go with a list, and never to the grocery store while hungry.
- Use the freezer. Anything you won't eat in a few days goes in and gets a date on it.

5. Food safety

This matters more as we age, because an infection that a younger person would shake off can make an older person very unwell.

- Wash hands for 20 seconds before cooking and after handling raw meat.
- Cook poultry to 74°C (165°F), ground meat to 71°C (160°F) and whole cuts of beef, pork and lamb to 63°C (145°F), with a rest.
- Raw meat stays in sealed bags on the bottom shelf, so it cannot drip on the food below.
- Thaw in the fridge, in cold water or in the microwave, never on the bench.
- Leftovers go into the fridge within two hours, and are eaten within three or four days.
- Reheat leftovers until they are steaming hot all the way through.
- A warm, wet sponge and a soft, moist food are where bacteria grow fastest. Change the sponge often, dry it between uses, and wash it hot.
- If you are on a low-sodium diet, remember that canned soups and ready meals are often very salty. Rinse canned beans and vegetables, or choose low-sodium cans.

6. Meal timings

Eat every 3 to 4 hours while awake. A small snack every few hours is often easier than three large meals.

Have protein at breakfast. Porridge with milk and yogurt, or eggs on toast, are examples. A protein-poor breakfast leaves you hungry by lunch and makes it harder to reach your daily total.

If you take insulin or tablets for diabetes, eat at the times your doctor has set. A missed meal with these medicines can be dangerous.

Some people do better with lunch at midday and dinner early. An early dinner is often easier on the heart and on the stomach at night.

7. Diabetes

The main aim is steady blood sugar, without going low.

Choose slow-digesting carbs: beans, lentils, whole grains, most fruit and vegetables. Eat less of the fast ones: white bread, white rice, sugary drinks and sweets.
Combine them. Carbohydrate with protein and fat digests more slowly, and a banana with some peanut butter is better than a banana on its own.
Keep the portions steady from day to day, and check your blood sugar as your doctor has set.
Watch the hidden sugars, in sauces, in flavored yogurt and in drinks called "fruit juice."
If you eat less than usual because of a bad day or a poor appetite, ask your doctor whether you should take less insulin or tablet on that day.

8. High blood pressure

The DASH eating plan is built for this: lots of vegetables, fruit, beans, low-fat dairy, fish, poultry and nuts, with little red meat, sweets and saturated fat.
Cut the salt. Most of it comes from bread, pasta sauce, soup, cured meats, cheese and ready meals. Cook at home, and taste before you salt.
Read labels. "Low sodium" means less than 140 mg per serving. "Reduced sodium" means less than the usual amount, and may still be high.
Drink less alcohol, or none. Three glasses of wine a day raises blood pressure in many people, and so does skipping a night.
If you take a diuretic, ask your doctor which foods to eat and which to avoid.

9. Heart disease

Limit saturated fat, from red meat, butter, cream, cheese and coconut oil, and avoid trans fat, which is listed on labels in many countries.
Eat fish twice a week, especially oily fish like salmon, mackerel and sardines.
Add nuts, seeds and olive oil.
Keep a healthy weight, and move every day, even if it is only walking. Ask your doctor what is safe for you.
If you have had a heart attack or a stent, follow your doctor's plan exactly.

10. A sample week

Monday: Oatmeal made with milk, topped with yogurt, banana and a spoon of peanut butter. Lunch: tuna and bean salad with olive oil and lemon. Dinner: chicken and vegetable stew, with crusty bread. Snack: an apple and some cheese.
Tuesday: Two scrambled eggs, a slice of wholegrain toast, sliced tomato. Lunch: leftover stew. Dinner: baked salmon, mashed potato and steamed greens. Snack: Greek yogurt.
Wednesday: Greek yogurt with berries and a few nuts. Lunch: lentil soup, a slice of wholegrain bread and a salad. Dinner: chicken and bean chili, with rice. Snack: a piece of fruit.
Thursday: Omelette with spinach, tomato and feta. Lunch: leftover chili. Dinner: pasta with tomato, garlic, olive oil and a little parmesan. Snack: cottage cheese and cucumber.
Friday: Porridge with milk, a poached egg on top and some grated apple stirred in. Lunch: tuna and bean salad. Dinner: roasted chicken thighs, roast potato, carrots and cabbage. Snack: a piece of fruit.
Weekend: Soup and a sandwich on whichever day is easiest. Fish on the other.

11. When to see a doctor

See a doctor if you have lost weight without trying, if you are often tired or dizzy, if you have trouble swallowing, if you have sores in your mouth or your teeth hurt, if you are not hungry for a week or more, or if you have questions about your medications. A dietitian can build a plan around your health, your budget and what you actually like to eat, which is the part you will keep.
