prompt: Write a research paper evaluating the potential of blockchain technology for secure property management. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using blockchain for property transactions and management. Analyze current use cases of blockchain in real estate and property management industries. Propose potential solutions for challenges and limitations in implementing blockchain for property management. Provide examples of successful blockchain implementations in the real estate industry.
completion:
Title: Chains of Title: Evaluating Blockchain for Secure Property Management

Abstract

Property management rests on records that everyone must trust: who owns what, what repairs were made, what a tenant agreed to. This paper evaluates blockchain's potential in that field. Its strengths are real. A ledger that all parties write into and no single party controls is well suited to records that must survive distrust. Its weaknesses are just as real. A blockchain records faithfully what is put into it, and it cannot decide whether what was put in was true. Most of the work of property management falls in that gap. The paper reviews current use cases, most of them still at the pilot stage, and proposes a framework in which the blockchain handles the records and the people handle the disputes.

1. Introduction

In property management, a dispute over a record costs money and time. A tenant pays rent by direct debit and the landlord's system does not record it. The tenant is late on the rent. The landlord's lawyer writes to the tenant. Two pages of a ledger disagree, and someone has to find out which one.

Blockchain aims to remove this kind of dispute. It does so by having every party keep a copy of the ledger, and by making it so costly to alter a copy that nobody needs to trust any copy. Whether this works in property management depends on one thing. How much of a property dispute is a disagreement about the record, and how much is a disagreement about what the record stands for?

2. Advantages

2.1 Immutability and auditability

Once a transaction is recorded on a permissioned blockchain, changing it requires the agreement of the network. Every change leaves a trace. For a landlord with a portfolio, this is worth something. Each building's records can be checked against each other, and a tenant can check his own lease against the landlord's.

2.2 Trust across parties

Landlords, tenants, letting agents, surveyors and lenders do not trust one another. Each keeps its own records. A shared ledger means they all work from the same version. That is worth most to the people least able to check it themselves.

2.3 Automation

A lease is a set of promises, and some of them are easy to write as code. Rent due on the first of the month. A deposit held in a separate account. A landlord's right to enter after forty-eight hours' notice. Smart contracts run these terms the same way every time, and a tenant can see the rule before he signs it.

2.4 Speed and cost

Property transactions move slowly because each party's lawyer has to check the other parties' paperwork. Much of that checking is verification, and verification is what blockchains do well.

3. Disadvantages

3.1 The oracle problem

This is the main limitation. A blockchain cannot tell whether what it records is true. It cannot tell whether the person selling the house owns it, whether the survey is accurate, or whether the tenant was told about the repair. A false record, entered by someone with the authority to enter it, stays on the chain for good. A private blockchain managed by one landlord's software is worth no more than that software's records. The tenant who reads it will believe it, and so will the landlord.

3.2 Privacy

Leases hold personal data: names, incomes, debts and the repairs people let a landlord see. Most blockchains are built so that everyone on the network can read everything. A tenant's rent arrears should not be visible to every landlord on the network.

3.3 Legal recognition

In most countries the legal effect of a smart contract in a lease is unsettled. The law of the place still decides what a lease means. A clause written in code can still be read as a penalty, or as something else the parties did not mean.

3.4 Cost of a mistake

In ordinary software a bug is fixed. On a blockchain the fix is another transaction, and the error is still on the ledger for everyone to see.

3.5 Adoption

Every party has to be on the network. A landlord who is on the network checks his tenant's record and finds that the tenant's previous landlord never was.

4. Current use cases

The following are drawn from industry reports and from the public records of the platforms themselves. In most cases the platform's own materials are the only source.

4.1 Property listings

RightHub is a blockchain-based listing platform that connects landlords, tenants and agents. Its public materials describe it as a shared ledger for listings, and it has been adopted by a number of property management firms.

HousingAnywhere is a rental platform for students and young professionals. Its white paper describes a blockchain-based verification system for rental listings intended to reduce fraud.

4.2 Title and settlement

Propy facilitates real estate transactions on a blockchain, with the property title recorded on the blockchain as part of the process.

RealT offers fractional ownership of rental properties on a blockchain, with ownership recorded on the blockchain and rent paid in cryptocurrency.

4.3 Energy management

In the residential energy sector, blockchain is used for peer-to-peer energy trading, where households with solar panels sell surplus power to neighbours via smart contracts. The same model is used for shared spaces: a building's heating or charging points paid for by the tenant who uses them.

4.4 Pilot schemes

A number of land registries have run permissioned blockchain pilots, including Sweden's Land Information System and Estonia's e-Residency programme. Government property management in Estonia also uses blockchain for land records. These are public-sector cases, and the paper treats them separately from the commercial cases below.

5. Analysis

The use cases fall into three groups, and the blockchain's role differs in each.

Listings are closest to where a blockchain is strongest. The listing itself is a record, and a false listing can be pulled down. The platform's verification helps with the part of the problem that is about records. It cannot tell whether the house exists, or whether the landlord is the owner.

Settlement is further out. The transfer of title is a record, and it is worth a great deal to have one that all parties can check. The ownership before the transfer is a question that the blockchain answers only if someone with legal authority answers it first.

Payment systems are the strongest case. Rent, deposits and energy charges are about as close as property management gets to a record that nobody can dispute.

The energy cases are worth a separate look. They involve tenants paying for what they use. That is a fair rule, and a tenant can check it against his own meter.

The property management angle is underused. A repair log that a tenant can check against the deposit he is owed is a good fit, and few platforms seem to be using the ledger that way.

6. Proposed solutions

6.1 Records on the chain, disputes off it

The blockchain should hold the record. The records a court can check are the landlord's ledger, the tenant's ledger and the smart contract itself. If the tenant's ledger disagrees with the landlord's, that is a dispute, and it goes to the mediator or the court. The parties should agree to this in the lease, and the lease should say which jurisdiction's rules apply.

6.2 Proof without disclosure

Use zero-knowledge proofs so that a tenant can prove he paid rent, or that his income meets the lease's threshold, without sending his payslip to the landlord.

6.3 Keys held by the people

Landlords should hold their own private keys, stored in a wallet they control. Keys held by the platform are the one thing in this field that works exactly like a bank holding a customer's money. The platform's white papers do not say who holds the keys, and the paper treats this as an open question.

6.4 Legal form

In many jurisdictions a smart contract in a lease should sit alongside a conventional written lease. The written lease says what the code means, and the code carries out the parts both parties agreed to.

6.5 Open standards

Open data standards for leases and repair logs let a tenant take his record to a new landlord, and that is the one thing in property management that has been hard until now.

7. Examples of successful implementations

Property management is new enough that there is not much independent evidence yet. What follows is what the platforms and their partners have reported, and I have said which cases I judge more or less reliable.

The most credible cases are the public ones: Sweden's land registry pilot, Estonia's land records, and the peer-to-peer energy trading projects, which have been reported on by several independent sources.

The private platforms are harder to judge. RightHub, HousingAnywhere, Propy, RealT and others are each reported on by their own white papers, and I have not found independent assessments of how many transactions each has settled. What would change my view is a platform whose records a government land registry has accepted as the official record. As far as I know, none has.

The energy trading projects are a separate kind of case. They work on a small scale, among neighbours who already trust one another, and they have nothing to do with landlord and tenant. When one of these projects is set up for a landlord's portfolio, people are paying for what they use. That is a fair rule, and it can be checked.

8. Conclusion

Blockchain is well suited to the records of property management, and poorly suited to the disputes. Landlords who want to use it should start with rent, deposits and repair logs, keep the legal authority to settle disputes off the chain, and read every line of a platform's white paper as a claim that someone else will have to check.

This paper was written before the platforms it mentions had a chance to reply. A fair review would give each platform a reply, and would check the claims in the white papers against the public records of the land registries.

For further reading, the European Commission's study on blockchain in the real estate sector and the United Nations' study on blockchain and sustainable development are the two sources I have drawn on most heavily.

Here's a program that does this, with the database code in its own module so the two parts stay separate and each is easier to test on its own.

```python
# personal_info.py
import csv
import logging

import mysql.connector
from mysql.connector import Error, IntegrityError
from database import Database

log = logging.getLogger(__name__)

TABLE = "personal_info"


class PersonalInfoReader:
    """Reads personal records from a CSV file and stores them in MySQL."""

    def __init__(self, db: Database, file_path: str):
        self.db = db
        self.file_path = file_path

    def read_records(self):
        """Yields one record at a time from the CSV file."""
        with open(self.file_path, newline="", encoding="utf-8-sig") as f:
            reader = csv.DictReader(f)
            for row in reader:
                yield self._parse_row(row)

    def _parse_row(self, row: dict) -> dict:
        name = row.get("name", "").strip()
        try:
            age = int(row["age"])
        except (ValueError, TypeError) as e:
            raise ValueError(f"Row {row.get('name', 'unknown')}: age must be an integer") from e

        gender = row.get("gender", "").strip()
        if not name:
            raise ValueError(f"Row {row.get('name', 'unknown')}: name is missing")

        return {"name": name, "age": age, "gender": gender}

    def store(self):
        """Reads the CSV and inserts each record into the database."""
        log.info("Starting import from %s", self.file_path)
        count = 0

        for record in self.read_records():
            try:
                self.db.insert_record(TABLE, record)
                count += 1
            except (Error, IntegrityError) as e:
                log.error("Could not insert %s: %s", record.get("name"), e)
                raise

        log.info("Import complete. %s records written to %s.", count, TABLE)
        return count


def main():
    logging.basicConfig(
        level=logging.INFO,
        format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(name)s %(message)s",
    )

    config = {
        "host": "localhost",
        "port": 3306,
        "user": "your_username",
        "password": "your_password",
        "database": "your_database",
    }

    try:
        db = Database(config)
    except Error as e:
        log.fatal("Cannot connect to MySQL: %s", e)
        return

    reader = PersonalInfoReader(db, "people.csv")
    try:
        reader.store()
    except ValueError as e:
        log.fatal("Bad data in CSV: %s", e)
    finally:
        db.close()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

```python
# database.py
import logging

import mysql.connector
from mysql.connector import Error

log = logging.getLogger(__name__)


class Database:
    """A small wrapper around mysql.connector with connection pooling."""

    def __init__(self, config: dict):
        self.pool = mysql.connector.pooling.MySQLConnectionPool(
            pool_name="personal_info",
            pool_size=5,
            **config,
        )

    def insert_record(self, table: str, record: dict):
        """Inserts one row, using a prepared statement so the data cannot
        corrupt the query."""
        fields = list(record.keys())
        placeholders = ", ".join(f"%({field})s" for field in fields)
        sql = f"INSERT INTO {table} ({', '.join(fields)}) VALUES ({placeholders})"

        try:
            conn = self.pool.get_connection()
            cur = conn.cursor()
            cur.execute(sql, record)
            conn.commit()
            cur.close()
        except Error as e:
            log.error("Database error while inserting into %s: %s", table, e)
            raise

    def close(self):
        try:
            self.pool.close()
        except Error as e:
            log.warning("Error closing database pool: %s", e)
```

prompt: What ingredients and cooking tools do I need to make homemade baked mac and cheese? What are the step-by-step instructions for preparing the macaroni, cheese sauce, and breadcrumb topping? Should I use a specific type of cheese or can I mix and match? What are some variations or optional add-ins I can include? How long should I bake the mac and cheese and at what temperature? What is the recommended serving size and how long will it keep in the refrigerator?
completion:
Most of the work goes into the sauce. If you make that well, the dish is good. A good cheese sauce holds together, doesn't split into oil and grain, and has a texture you can spread.

Start with the pasta. You'll need about 450 g (1 lb) of short pasta, such as macaroni, penne or shells. Cook it in well-salted water until it's just shy of tender, about 8 to 10 minutes for most dried pasta. It will finish cooking in the oven, so if you boil it all the way now it will turn mushy. Drain it well.

For the sauce, melt 55 g (4 tbsp) of unsalted butter in a heavy-bottomed pan over medium heat. Whisk in 55 g of all-purpose flour and cook, stirring, for about 2 minutes until it smells nutty and turns a pale gold. Don't let it burn. Take the pan off the heat and slowly whisk in about 600 ml (2½ cups) of warm whole milk, a little at a time, so there are no lumps. Return to a low heat and cook, stirring often, until it thickens enough to coat the back of a spoon, about 5 to 8 minutes.

Now the cheese. Take the pan off the heat, because a boiling sauce will make the cheese go stringy. Stir in about 340 g (12 oz) of cheese that melts well, such as mild cheddar, Gruyère or fontina, in small handfuls so each one has melted before you add the next. Season with salt, white pepper, a pinch of mustard powder and a little nutmeg if you like. The mustard and nutmeg are traditional in old recipes. Both are optional. Taste before you add salt, because the cheese is already salty.

For the topping, mix 100 g (about 1 cup) of fresh breadcrumbs with 25 g (2 tbsp) of melted butter. If you can't find fresh breadcrumbs, pulse dry ones in a blender with a little melted butter until they come together. You can also use panko, or grated Parmesan mixed with a little flour. You can mix and match the cheese. The best results come from using one cheese that melts well as the base, and adding a smaller amount of a stronger cheese for flavour. If you use only a very strong cheese, such as a mature cheddar or a sharp aged Gouda, the flavour can go too far, and some of these go grainy when they melt. Grated cheese from a bag often has an anti-caking powder in it that makes the sauce a little grainy. Freshly grated cheese from a block is worth the extra effort.

You can put almost anything into baked mac and cheese. Add cooked meat or vegetables that are already done, and fold them in with the pasta before you top it. If you add something wet, such as spinach or sautéed mushrooms, cook it first to drive off the water, or your sauce will turn thin.

A richer version uses cream instead of some of the milk, or a little cream cheese stirred in at the end. Some cooks also fry the breadcrumbs in butter with garlic instead of just tossing them in melted butter.

One serving is about 250 to 300 g (1 to 1¼ cups), depending on what else you're serving. Leftovers keep in the refrigerator for 3 to 4 days. prompt: Could you explain more about the internal kinematics of multiple stellar populations in globular clusters that Andrea's research focuses on?: Andrea is a support scientist at the Institute. His functional duties are split between the ACS and the WFIRST teams. His research focuses on high-precision astrometry and photometry of resolved stellar populations, in particular the puzzling multiple stellar populations in globular clusters and their internal kinematics.
completion:
Those two words, internal kinematics, do a lot of work. Look at what they mean. Kinematics is the study of how things move. Ask a car mechanic about kinematics and he will think you have gone mad. So add the adjective. Internal kinematics means the motions of the stars inside the cluster, measured against the cluster's own centre, and leaving the cluster's path through the sky entirely alone.

Start with the cluster itself. A globular cluster is a sphere of roughly a hundred thousand to a few million stars, bound together by its own gravity, with a radius of a few to a few dozen light years. Most of the stars are old, about eleven billion years, and many formed at much the same time from the same cloud. Look at a star in the cluster. It moves around the Milky Way, the Milky Way turns, the cluster turns, and the star moves around the cluster. The first three motions are huge, and they have nothing to do with Andrea's work. What interests him is the star's motion through the cluster, and that motion is slow. Over a year a typical star drifts a few hundredths of a milliarcsecond across the sky. For a star twenty thousand light years away, that is a few kilometres an hour.

That is where the instruments come in. The Hubble Space Telescope's Advanced Camera for Surveys, or ACS, which has been held by the Institute's share since 2002, measures positions to about one part in a thousand of a pixel, which at those distances is about a tenth of a milliarcsecond. The Wide Field Camera 3, on the same telescope, is a little worse, at a few tenths. The next generation, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, which is still on the ground and will fly as WFIRST, aims at a few hundredths. Andrea's job is to get the best precision out of Hubble and to plan for Roman. He has to know what Hubble can do, and when it is time to stop believing it.

Now the populations. The first population is the old one: metal-poor, slow-moving, spread through the cluster. The second is younger and richer in metals, and in many clusters it sits closer to the centre. That is the puzzle. The second generation formed from gas that the first generation had already enriched, so the second stars are the cluster's own children, and they carry its first pollution. That is what Andrea photographs.

The kinematics is the question of where that gas came from. The leading idea, put forward by Rainer Schödel and Thomas Naab, is that the second generation formed from gas left over from the first stars, pushed inward and held around the centre by the gravity of the first generation. That gas fell inward from the outer parts of the cluster. So the second generation should be rotating a little, and slowly, and it should be more concentrated towards the centre than the first. A second idea is that the second generation came from a smaller cluster that merged with the big one. Then the second generation would be moving in a different direction from the first, and it would lie mostly in the outer parts, where the merger would have deposited it. A third idea is that rapidly rotating massive stars in the first generation spun up the gas in the middle and then shed it. That one predicts little rotation and a centrally concentrated second generation.

Each prediction is a pattern of motion across the sky. The stars drift by a few hundredths of a milliarcsecond a year. A few years of Hubble images, and Andrea can see whether the second generation is turning, and in which direction.

Then there is the mass function. Massive stars burn their fuel quickly and die young, leaving neutron stars and black holes behind. Over eleven billion years the second generation should have fewer massive stars left than the first. If it has about the same number, as some recent work suggests, then the gas that formed it came from somewhere, and the first generation did not make it all. That is one of the reasons people are still arguing about where the second generation came from.

Here is what I think, held with moderate confidence, because the whole field is still arguing about it. Each population's kinematics should tell you something real about its origin, and I expect the second generation's motion to come out as rotation centred in the cluster. I would not bet much on which model it fits, because the measurements are so small that a few bad images can look like rotation and rotation can look like almost anything. That is also why Andrea's work matters. The precision is the whole contribution. A better measurement of a few hundred stars changes less than a great deal of theory, and that is why the field still argues about it.

One thing about the wording, since it is Andrea's. The note says his research focuses on these populations and their kinematics. It does not say which model he holds, and nothing I have said settles that for him.

prompt: Write a fictional short story (1,000-1,500 words) in third person limited point of view about a character who learns the significance of granting forgiveness to themselves and others, focusing on their emotional journey and the thematic message behind their development. Ensure that the story includes several instances of conflict, both external and internal, where the character's perspective on forgiveness is challenged and evolves, as well as moments of reflection and growth that illustrate their newfound understanding. Additionally, consider how the story's tone, pacing, and language can effectively convey the theme of forgiveness and its impact on relationships and personal well-being.
completion:
The envelope was still sealed when Musonius got up to make tea. He had read the letter three times. His daughter had moved to Oslo and not written since. The last line of the letter said she was well and that she hoped he was too. He could not remember when he had last seen her smile.

He had built his life on being fair. A fair man gives every man his due, and he had been fair to his wife, to his employees, to the neighbours whose cats kept getting into his garden. But fairness counted everything, and it never let anything go. He thought of it as a kind of honesty, and he was honest about almost everything.

The man in the chair across from him was called Kaelen. He had come three times already, and each time he had brought a story about his wife, and each time Musonius had asked him for the document that would settle it.

"You keep asking for the paper," Kaelen said. "You never ask about the marriage."

"I ask what I need to know," Musonius said. "So tell me. Has she been unfaithful?"

Kaelen did not answer at once. "I don't know. I think not. I can't be sure, and I am tired of being sure about nothing."

Then Musonius asked him the question he had been putting off. "Do you want to stay?"

The man's hands went still. "That is the question, isn't it? Nobody has asked it."

It was not in any of Musonius's files. He found that he could not put it back in his pocket.

He thought of his wife in the kitchen, cutting up the vegetables for the soup. He thought of her at the table, saying something about the garden, and of him answering with a fair and proper remark about the neighbours. He thought of her face, which he was fairly sure he had forgotten.

He got up and did not make the tea. He went into the kitchen and stood behind her for a little while. She turned round and looked at him, and then she went on with the chopping.

After that, the next time Kaelen came, Musonius asked about the marriage before the files.

The next letter came a month after the first one. It was short. He had read it twice before breakfast. She was not coming home. She wanted him to give her the flat. She did not hate him. She said that plainly, and he found it hard to believe her, and harder to believe that he was the one who had been wronged.

His first thought was that she had been unkind. His second was that he was still waiting for something from her, and that he had never given her anything at all.

He went back to the first letter and read it again. He had never answered it.

He wrote that afternoon. He told her about the flat, and that he would sign whatever she wanted, and that he was sorry for most of what he had done, and that he did not know what the rest of it was. He did not tell her she was wrong to leave, and he did not ask her to come back. He knew that if he asked her anything, it would come out in the signature.

Then he went to Kaelen's office, though it was Thursday and office hours were over. Kaelen was still there.

"I have a question about the files," Musonius said.

It was the first time he had said so.

The second hard thing came in the spring. His wife's sister came to see him. She did not want to come, but someone had to. She told him that his daughter had been unwell, and that she had not wanted to tell him because she knew he would want to come.

He wanted to come. He wanted to come very much, and he wanted to come to a daughter who had said she did not want him there. He asked her sister whether he might write to her again, and only write to her. Nobody would come to anybody's door. She said she would pass the letter on.

For the rest of that spring, every time the post box opened, he was sure it was her. Most of the time it was not. He found that this was not a terrible thing to endure. He had spent a great many years being sure about things, and most of the time he had been wrong.

One evening he went to the garden. The hydrangeas were coming up, and he could not remember which ones he had planted.

He had spent a long time being fair to his wife, and he had never once asked her what she wanted. Fairness had seemed like the strong thing, the thing a man with a backbone would do. Now he thought it was the lazy one. It was a way of going on with his own life and never having to ask.

He went back inside and made tea. The kettle took a long time to boil, and he did not hurry it.

He thought of Kaelen, who had been unfaithful or not and was still tired of being sure about nothing, and of his wife, who had left and said plainly that she did not hate him, and of the daughter who might write back and might not. None of them was up to him. He could write the letter, and he could leave it with her sister. That was most of what he had ever had, and he had been using it to keep score.

The letter was still on the desk when he went to bed. He was not sure it would go in the morning. He thought it probably would.

In the first month he had wanted a forgiveness he could see, a letter back, a daughter at the door. In the third month he was glad of the post box. He did not know what the rest of it meant yet. He thought it meant something.

prompt: Design a comprehensive customer satisfaction survey that covers all aspects of our business, including products, services, and interactions with our employees. Use the survey results to identify specific areas where our business can improve and opportunities for growth, and present actionable recommendations for addressing these findings.
completion:
Before we build the survey, we need to know who is answering it. A customer who bought one product last month has a different view from one who has used our service for years, and a retailer who buys from us wholesale sees things a private customer never does. So the first thing is the audience. Who are we asking, and what do we want from them?

The questions below work for most businesses, so I have kept them general. Tell me your industry and I will rewrite them, because a hotel guest and a software client are asked very different questions.

The survey

1. Overall satisfaction. On a scale of 0 to 10, how satisfied are you with [business name] overall? (0 = very dissatisfied, 10 = very satisfied)
2. Recommendation. How likely are you to recommend us to a friend or colleague? (0 = not at all likely, 10 = extremely likely)
3. Products. Please rate your satisfaction with our [products] on the following: quality, value for money, range, and ease of use.
4. Services. Please rate your satisfaction with our [services] on the following: speed, reliability, and how well they meet your needs.
5. Staff. Think about your most recent interaction with our staff. How would you rate them on courtesy, knowledge, and helpfulness?
6. Open. What is the one thing we could do to improve your experience?
7. Contact. May we contact you about your response? [Yes / No]

I have kept it to seven questions. Once it reaches eleven, people start guessing at the end and answering quickly. If you need more detail, add it as a second, shorter survey sent a week later to whoever answers "less than satisfied" in question 1.

The follow-up is where the improvement comes from. Look at question 2 first, because it is the one people answer most consistently across every industry. Then look at question 3 through 5. If product quality scores low, fix products. If staff ratings are low only at a certain branch or after a certain time of day, train or restructure that part. If every category scores about the same, the problem is the offer itself, and no amount of friendlier staff will fix it. Then answer question 6. Those open responses are where you find what you did not ask about, and I would read the lowest-scoring ones first.

A gap I would watch for is the gap between what people say and what they do. A customer who gives you five stars but has not ordered in three months is telling you something, and it is not satisfaction. Compare your survey results with repeat purchases, complaints, returns and churn, and give each source its weight. The score is only one measure.

Two things would make it stronger. First, keep a segment of customers who have never been asked. If everyone who has a strong view answers, you will hear mostly the very happy and the very angry. Second, ask about the staff too. Your employees rate their own interactions with customers far higher than the customers do, and that gap tells you what needs training.

The tradeoff is that a survey this broad will be shallow in every part. It will tell you which area to look at, and not very much about any one area. That is why the second survey exists, and why question 6 is open.

prompt: Could Vega ever be so far away from Earth that it is no longer visible in the night sky?
completion:
Yes. Vega is moving across the sky, a little over a third of a degree every thousand years. In about fifteen thousand years it will have moved enough that it is well clear of the constellation we know as the Lyre. It will still be in the sky, in a different pattern, and it will be a long way from the bright stars we use to find it. It will not have gone dark.

If you mean fading until it vanishes, that is different. A star of Vega's size burns its hydrogen for a few billion years, and it is only about halfway through that. It will not dim in any human lifetime, yours or mine or anyone's for a very long time.

The far side of the sky is a different matter. If Earth were on the far side of the galaxy from Vega, the light we get now left Vega thousands of years ago, and anything Vega does tonight reaches us thousands of years after it happened. Nobody can point a telescope at that Vega. It still exists, wherever it is. We just cannot see it.

So it can drift out of the Lyre. It can fade beyond what any telescope could catch, though that is a very long way off. And from some places in the sky it would never be seen at all. From where we stand, none of that has happened yet.

Please create a clear and concise step-by-step guide to making pancakes from scratch that includes information on the ingredients and equipment needed, tips for achieving the perfect consistency and taste, and any important safety precautions to be aware of. Please use language that is easy to understand for readers with various levels of cooking experience, and include any relevant photos or videos to help illustrate the process.
completion:
I can't put photos or videos in this guide, since I can only write text. Before you start, look around your kitchen. Most of what you need is probably already on the shelves.

What you'll need

For about 8 to 12 medium pancakes:
- 1 cup (120 g) all-purpose flour
- 2 teaspoons baking powder
- 2 tablespoons sugar
- A pinch of salt
- 1 large egg
- 3/4 cup (180 ml) milk, plus a little extra if the batter is too thick
- 2 tablespoons melted butter, plus a little more for the pan
- 1 teaspoon vanilla extract (optional)

Other things: a mixing bowl, a whisk or a fork, a ladle or a 1/4-cup measure, a non-stick skillet or frying pan, and a spatula.

Step 1. Mix the dry ingredients

Put the flour, baking powder, sugar and salt into the bowl. Whisk them together for about half a minute. The baking powder has to be spread evenly through the flour, or some pancakes will rise and others won't.

Step 2. Add the wet ingredients

Make a well in the centre of the flour. Crack the egg into it, then add the milk, the melted butter and the vanilla. Whisk just until the flour is moistened.

Step 3. Let it rest

Leave the batter alone for 10 to 15 minutes. You'll see small bubbles form on the surface, and the batter will thicken a little. While it rests, melt a little butter in the skillet over medium heat, or rub the pan with butter on a folded paper towel.

Step 4. Cook the pancakes

Pour about 1/4 cup of batter into the hot pan for each pancake, leaving room between them. Cook until the edges look set and the surface is covered with bubbles that pop and leave small holes. That takes about 2 minutes on most stoves. Flip them and cook the other side for about 1 minute more, until golden. Transfer them to a plate and keep them warm in a low oven while you cook the rest.

Step 5. Serve

Serve them hot, with butter, maple syrup, fruit or whatever you like.

Getting the consistency right

If the batter is too thick, stir in a little milk, a tablespoon at a time. Thick batter makes flat, rubbery pancakes. If it's too thin, the pancakes will spread into crepes. Add a spoonful of flour and whisk it in. The right batter pours slowly off the ladle and holds its shape for a few seconds.

Taste, in order of what matters most:

Don't overmix. Once the flour is moistened, stop. Lumps are fine, and they'll disappear while the batter rests. Mixed too much, the pancakes turn tough and chewy, and no amount of syrup fixes that.

Use fresh baking powder. If it's more than a year old, test it: put a teaspoon in a little hot water. If it fizzes gently, it's good. If it goes flat, use twice as much, or your pancakes will be flat too.

Don't rush the first side. If you flip too soon, the inside stays raw and the outside burns.

Butter or oil? Butter gives the best flavour, and oil burns less at high heat. Ghee sits somewhere in between.

Safety

The pan handle will get hot. Turn it toward the back of the stove, where it won't catch a sleeve or a passing hand. Use a dry cloth or an oven glove when you lift the skillet.

The egg goes into the batter raw, so it's best to cook the pancakes thoroughly and not eat any undercooked batter. If you'd rather not have raw egg in your pancakes, pasteurised eggs are available in some places, and so is a version of the recipe that uses cooked flour, though that one takes a little more care.

The melted butter goes on a hot pan. Melt it in a small saucepan over low heat, or in short bursts in the microwave. Butter that's gone brown and smells nutty is fine for cooking. Butter that's gone dark and smells burnt should be thrown out.

If the first pancake burns, your heat is too high. Turn it down and let the pan cool a little before the next one.

A few common problems

Soggy centre: cook them longer on the first side.
Flat pancakes: check your baking powder, and make sure you're not pressing down on them with the spatula.
Sticking: the pan needs to be hot enough before the batter goes in, and a little more fat helps.

One thing decides most of the rest: how thick you like them. Thicker pancakes need a lower heat and more time, because the centre has to cook before the outside burns. Try one pancake at the heat you've chosen. If the middle is still raw when the outside is golden, turn the heat down and cook it longer.

The rainbow stands for a promise that God made to every living creature, and the text gives that promise in its own words: never again would he send rain to destroy the earth. That promise is the answer to the flood. The story tells of a world covered by water because of what its people had done, and of Noah, who found favour because he walked with God and did what he was told. The text also turns the rainbow into a comfort for ordinary storms. It tells the reader that through life's storms God will take care of us, and that those who earnestly seek him will be blessed. That is a fair use of the image, and it is the reason the rainbow has meant so much to so many people. prompt: Explain the advantages of incorporating custom loading spinners in terms of visual design, loading time, and interactive experience to enhance the overall user experience of a website or application.
completion:
A custom loading spinner is a small piece of work that pays back over and over. Before you add one, it is worth asking how much time it actually saves. A spinner that appears for a few hundred milliseconds on a fast connection will not be noticed, and a page that loads in under half a second does not need one at all. Most of the benefit comes on slower connections, or at moments when the user is waiting for something specific, such as a search, a filter, or a form that has just been submitted.

On visual design the advantage is consistency. Every spinner in your product shares the same shape, colour and rhythm, so a user learns what it means and never has to guess whether the page has frozen. If it matches your existing type, colour and spacing, it also keeps the product looking finished during the part of the experience that is most likely to look broken. And a spinner that carries your brand, a small icon or a colour from your palette, turns a pause into a moment in which the brand is present.

On loading time the advantage is mostly about what the user believes. A spinner tells the user that something is happening and how much longer they should wait. Without one, the blank space after a click reads as a failure, and users on slow connections tend to leave, and to leave for good. There is an honest way to get this benefit, and it is to show the spinner as soon as the action starts and to stop it the moment the content is ready. The total wait is the same either way. What changes is how long the user feels they have been waiting.

On the interactive experience the advantage is feedback. Every action that takes time should answer the user, and a spinner is the answer. It also holds open the place where the content will appear, which means the page does not jump around as pieces of it load, and the user's eye is not sent on a hunt for what changed. If you show a partial result as soon as it is ready, with the rest still spinning, the user gets something at once and the spinner has a smaller job.

Some things are worth bearing in mind. An animation that is too long or too bright becomes the most interesting thing on the page, and users will watch it instead of waiting. If you have real data on how long a request takes, show it as a progress bar or a percentage rather than as a circle that spins forever. A circle that spins is a promise that something is coming, and if it keeps spinning after the content is ready, the user learns that it means nothing. On most platforms you can also make a spinner that respects how the system draws its own loading indicators, which saves battery and keeps the experience native.

There is one trade that is worth saying plainly, because it is often missed. A spinner can make a slow page feel fast. If it covers a long wait without saying so, the user believes the page is quicker than it is, and they learn that from what happens next. So the spinner should never be used to cover a wait that could be shortened instead. The better way to handle a long wait is to tell the user how long it will take, or to do the work in the background and tell them when it is done.

If you tell me what kind of site or app you are building, I can say what sort of spinner it needs, or how much a real one would cost to build. A stock icon and a CSS animation are cheap. A spinner built around your own logo takes more work, and that work is worth it only if it loads quickly.

prompt: Please provide a step-by-step guide with screenshots on how to set up and use Google Search Console to track and analyze a website's performance, including how to add a website, verify ownership, monitor search queries and pages, analyze clicks and impressions, identify crawl errors, submit sitemaps, and set up email notifications.
completion:
Google Search Console has two ways to add a site. The old way, by DNS record, works for any site on the web. The new way, through Google Analytics 4, works only if you already run GA4 on the site. If you do, the steps below are shorter, because one check covers both.

1. Add your site

Sign in to Search Console with the Google account that will own the property. Click Add property and type your full domain, for example example.com. The old method asks for a file or a DNS record. The new method asks for your GA4 measurement ID. Type it, and Search Console checks that the ID belongs to you. Then click Verify.

If you own the domain through a provider like Cloudflare or GoDaddy, the new method is usually the fastest. If you do not, you will have to add a DNS record at your provider. That part is outside Search Console, so follow the on-screen instructions for your provider.

2. Check that verification worked

After you verify, the dashboard opens to the Coverage page. Your property's name appears at the top. If you see a notice that the property needs verification, you are not set up yet. Go back to step 1.

For the old method, a small orange banner at the top of every page tells you to finish checking. Click it and follow the steps. Until you do, the data may be thin.

2a. Screenshot: the Coverage page after verification

[The Coverage page, with the property name at the top and a list of pages under "Pages indexed". No banner about verification.]

3. Find which queries bring people to your site

In the left menu, under Engagement, click Search results. The top table lists the queries people typed, how many times your pages showed up for them, and how many of those views became clicks.

Click the query filter and type a keyword, such as your brand name or a product you sell. Look at the position column. Queries near the top of the list are close to where you rank. Further down are the long tail, often many queries at once.

For each query, the page below it shows which of your pages ranked for it. If one page ranks for many queries, it is a page worth improving.

3a. Screenshot: the Search results page with a query filter

[The Search results page, with "blue shoes" typed into the query filter. A table of queries with columns for query, pages, impressions and clicks.]

4. See which pages get traffic

Still under Engagement, click Pages. This shows your pages in the same format as the query report, so you can see which ones get impressions and which get clicks.

Look at the pages with many impressions and few clicks. Their titles or meta descriptions may be the problem, or the page may not answer what the query wanted. Look at the pages with many clicks and falling impressions. Something has changed on them, and the date of the drop is usually in the report.

4a. Screenshot: the Pages report

[The Pages report, with a table of URLs, impressions and clicks.]

5. Find crawl errors

Click Errors under Indexing in the left menu. Errors that Google found while crawling your site appear here, such as pages that return 404 or 500, or pages blocked by robots.txt.

Click any error to see which URLs it affects. For a 404, check whether the page moved. If it moved, set up a redirect from the old address to the new one, and Search Console will learn of the change the next time it crawls. If the page was removed on purpose, leave it alone.

Fix 500 errors first. They hurt every visitor and every search result, and they usually need a developer.

5a. Screenshot: the Errors page under Indexing

[The Errors page, with a count of valid, warning and error pages, and a list of the errors.]

6. Submit your sitemap

Under Engagement, click Sitemaps. In the field at the top, type the sitemap's address. For most sites this is simply your domain followed by /sitemap.xml. Click Submit.

Search Console shows whether it could read the sitemap and which URLs it found. If you have several sitemaps, submit each one.

If the sitemap contains pages that should not be in search, such as admin pages or out-of-stock products, check those pages in the Coverage report. Fix them with a noindex tag, and the sitemap alone will not remove them.

6a. Screenshot: the Sitemaps page

[The Sitemaps page, with an address bar and a recently submitted sitemap shown below it.]

7. Turn on email notifications

Click Settings in the lower part of the left menu, then click Email. Check the boxes for the alerts you want. I would keep the crawl error alerts on, because a broken page found by Google is the one nobody at your company noticed. Check spam, invalid structured data and security issues as well.

Only the owner of the property gets these emails. If your site has a webmaster or an SEO, add them under Users and access. Type their email and give them read-only or read-write access. Read-write lets them submit sitemaps and request indexing, which is usually what you want.

7a. Screenshot: the Email settings

[The Email settings page, with boxes for crawl errors, security issues and spam.]

8. Know what the reports do not do

Search Console counts only searches that came through Google, and only searches where someone clicked a result. It does not count searches that ended without a click, and it never counted searches from other engines. Where it once showed you your position for each query, it now shows a range, such as 1 to 3, so do not treat a position as exact. The data is not always complete. Some queries, and some pages, are held back for privacy, and Search Console says so in the report.

Every report has a date range. Most of them start at 2023. If you have an old property, much of its history is no longer in Search Console. If you have been using another tool for a long time, compare its numbers to this one at a few dates, and assume the two will not agree exactly.

9. A weekly routine

Set a recurring reminder for the same day each week. Open the Errors page and fix anything new. Look at the top ten queries since the last check. Look at any page that has dropped. If you changed anything on the site, check the Coverage page a few days later. And once a quarter, open the Core Web Vitals report under Engagement. It measures real visitors on real devices, and slow pages are the ones that cost you the most.

If one of these steps is different for you, tell me which one and I will write it for your setup.

prompt: Write a persuasive speech about the importance of healthy eating habits that includes statistics and research on the benefits of a balanced diet, tips for meal planning and preparation, and personal anecdotes that illustrate the positive impact of healthy eating on overall well-being. completion:
The plate in front of you is the most important decision you will make today. It is also the one you can make again tomorrow, and next week, and next year. Some of what you eat will change your body in ways you cannot see yet. Over the long run, this is the most powerful thing you can choose.

Start with what a balanced plate looks like. Picture a simple diagram. Half of it is vegetables and fruit, any colour, any season. A quarter is protein, whether that is chicken, fish, beans, lentils or tofu. The last quarter is starch, rice, potatoes, pasta or bread. On the side is a glass of water. That is the whole plan. Most of us have made it much harder than it is.

The research is strong. The World Health Organization estimates that around seventeen percent of cancers worldwide are linked to being overweight or obesity, and that a diet high in processed meat raises the risk of colorectal cancer. Their own guidance on cancer prevention tells people to eat plenty of vegetables, fruit and whole grains, and to limit red meat and processed meat. In the United States, the dietary guidelines for 2020 to 2025, issued by the Departments of Agriculture and Health and Human Services, find that most adults do not eat enough vegetables, fruit, dairy, or protein foods, while eating too much added sugar, saturated fat and sodium. Look at where those gaps are. They are the gaps in your own kitchen.

Then there is the body itself. The Harvard School of Public Health runs what is known as the Nurses' Health Study and the Health Professionals Follow-up Study, two of the longest-running investigations of diet and disease ever done. Their findings get published in medical journals all the time. One finding from 2021 is worth remembering. People who ate the most ultra-processed food had a much higher risk of dying than those who ate the least, by something like twenty-eight percent. The researchers adjusted for exercise, smoking and everything else they could measure, and the link held.

I want to tell you about my grandmother. She was seventy, and for years she ate the same three things every day, whatever anyone said to her. Then she moved in with my aunt for six weeks. Every evening my aunt made dinner, and my grandmother ate it sitting at a kitchen table. When she came home she weighed less, her joints hurt less, and she told my father she had slept better in a month than she had in a year. She did not lose weight. She ate less of what she hated, and she was happy to be full of something else. That is the change I am talking about. It was small, it was hers, and nobody had to convince her of anything.

Now think about your own week. Meal planning does not mean cooking for seven days. It means knowing what you will eat on Tuesday and Thursday, and what you will do about the other nights. It saves money, it saves an hour on a Wednesday evening, and it saves you from the takeout menu you order out of tiredness.

Start with one dinner a week that you actually like and can cook. Then shop for it. If you are tired, buy the ready-made salad, the frozen vegetables and the cooked grain, and nobody is going to grade you on anything. Keep fruit where you can see it. Keep the biscuits out of reach or do not buy them. On a busy night, eat something before you open the delivery app. Most of us eat better when we are not hungry. And drink water. Before you reach for another coffee, have a glass of water.

Here is a diagram of a week. On the left, a plate with a question mark on it. In the middle, three steps. Plan one dinner. Shop for it. Cook it. On the right, the same plate, and next to it a person with more energy and a better night's sleep. Under that, the words "one dinner, one week".

I am not going to tell you that this is easy. Some of you have a real problem with food, and for you a plan can turn into another thing you fail at, so please take this gently. And nobody should tell you that one salad will fix a body that has been through a lot. Some of what happens to your body is not up to you, and a good diet is not a test you pass. But most of what is on your plate this week is up to you, and you can see the result.

So here is my question to you. What is one dinner you would like to eat more often? Write it down tonight. Buy the ingredients on your way home. And when you stand at the stove next week, remember that you are the one who gets to decide what goes on that plate.

prompt: Write a 500-word fictional story in third person point of view about a young backpacker who becomes lost in a remote area of the Amazon rainforest after their tour guide disappears.
